name: Settings page
markup: No html in this file. Each variant below carries the path to its own markup at r/settings-page/<variant>.html — fetch the one you need.
description: The configuration screen: a permanent nav of sections down one side and the section being changed beside it. One h1 for the whole screen, an h2 per section, and a Save that belongs to the section rather than to the page.
when_to_use: Where a user goes to change one thing out of the forty that live there — company and plant details, the financial year, numbering series for POs and GRNs, approval limits, tax defaults, users and roles, and the master lists every other screen picks from. The line against form-page is what the user came to do. A form page is one record somebody came to fill in and submit: one Save, one dirty state, one exit, and when it is done they leave. Settings is a place. The nav never goes away, the Save is per section, a setting that takes effect the moment it is touched sits beside one that does not, and the accident this layout exists to catch is clicking a different section with changes still pending. Against tabs the test is the count and the address: tabs are two to seven sibling views of one record inside one document, switched by a widget that owns the arrow keys and marks itself with aria-selected. Past about six sections that row wraps, scrolls or turns into a select and stops being scannable — and a settings section is a URL, so its nav is a list of real links marked with aria-current="page" and the browser owns the keys. Against sidebar: sidebar is the application's own navigation and this screen renders inside it. The section nav is the second level and has to read as the second level. Do not assemble it out of sidebar, and do not lift the settings sections up into the application sidebar, where they push every operational destination below the fold. A screen that lists records somebody works through is data-table, and one switch on one record is toggle on that record's page.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every other signed-in screen, which is the whole design problem: two levels of navigation on one page. The section nav is deliberately the quieter of the two — a bare list with a 2px rule down its side, no icons, no fills, no counts, sitting on the page rather than in a panel of its own. Give it the sidebar's tinted current row and its icon column and the screen has two panels both claiming to be the navigation, at which point the user reads the nearer one as the application and gets lost between them.

Saving is per section and the button says which section it commits — Save approval limits, not Save. One Save over a nav of forty sections promises to write things the user cannot see and has never looked at, and the first time it does that in a numbering series nobody trusts the screen again.

The section footer is always on screen and never appears on the first keystroke. A bar that materialises when the form goes dirty adds 52px to the pane under the pointer at the exact moment somebody is typing in the last field. What arms is the line inside it, not the bar itself.

The dirty guard is per section and armed by input and change, exactly as form-page arms it. What is different is where it fires: the likely accident is not closing the tab, it is clicking Tax defaults while Approval limits has an edit in it, so the guard has to intercept the nav click as well as beforeunload. A guard that only covers the browser navigation catches the rare case and misses the common one.

Two promises on one screen, and they are never interleaved. A switch writes when it is touched; a field writes when Save is pressed. Put them in one run and the user cannot tell which gesture applies to which row, so they go in separate blocks under separate h3 headings with a divider between them, and the block of switches says once that there is nothing to save. When a section holds both, the Save moves out of the card footer to the end of the block it commits — a Save button sitting under a run of switches promises to save the switches.

Sections the user may not open are absent from the nav, not disabled in it. A greyed row advertises a section, refuses it, and gives no reason; and it is the one component in the page that a screen reader cannot reach to be told why. The filtering is the view's job — the template guard is the second lock, not the first, because the section still has a URL somebody can type.

Every section is a URL and the nav is real links. That is what lets an error message elsewhere in the application say where the rule lives — "orders above ₹5,00,000 need a second approver, set in Settings, Approval limits" — and link straight to it. A tablist cannot be linked into, and a settings screen that cannot be linked into gets explained in a wiki instead.

The numbering series preview is computed in the page from the same four fields the server concatenates, so the string the user is about to commit is the string they read. It is an <output>, never a disabled input, and the half that cannot be undone is gated by an acknowledgement with the actual next number printed in it rather than by a dialog that says Are you sure.

How many role columns a matrix can carry belongs to checkbox, not to this entry: checkbox/matrix up to three, checkbox/wide-matrix past that, with a frozen capability column and both axes pinned. This section shows the split-by-module arrangement, which is the other way to spend the room a settings pane has and reads better when the modules are genuinely separate concerns. Either is right here. What is never right is a second copy of the same boxes restacked for a phone, because two renderings of one checkbox is two values for one permission and after a save the hidden one is wrong — checkbox/wide-matrix-phone is a separate variant for exactly that reason.

Below lg the nav stacks above the pane in DOM order, which is honest for nine sections and nothing more. At 390px a permanent side nav cannot be permanent: the index and the section become two screens, and the Back control is a real link because in production those are two URLs.

The destructive section is last in the nav, below a rule, and it is a white card like every other section. The colour is in the icon and in the button, and the consequence is written out in figures — 34 orders, 61 invoices — because that sentence is what stops the click, not a red panel behind it.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and any dialog is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it is the shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, and make the dialog fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header unchanged: the one h1, which says Settings and not the name of the open section, and a line under it naming the company and the financial year everything on this screen is scoped to.

A <nav> with its own accessible name holding a list of real links, one per section, marked with aria-current="page". A 2px zinc-700 rule and font-medium mark the open one; there is no fill, because the fill is what the application sidebar uses and there are two navs on this screen.
A search input above the nav on a deployment with more than about fifteen sections. It hides rows in the nav and never touches the pane, and it reports how many of the total are left.
The single column beside the nav holding exactly one section. A <section> labelled by its own h2, with tabindex="-1" so the keyboard follows a nav click into it.
card's shape: header with the h2 and one line saying what the section governs, body, footer. Blocks inside it are h3 and divided with border-zinc-100 — cards do not nest.
Always present. Left, who changed the section last and when, and the role="status" line the save answers into. Right, Discard then Save, and the Save names the section.

The run of toggles that write when they are touched, under their own h3, with one line saying there is nothing to save and one role="status" line under the run. Never mixed into the run of fields above it.

The per-section dirty flag, the alert-dialog it raises when a nav link is clicked with changes pending, and the beforeunload that covers the tab closing. Three answers, and focus lands on Keep editing.
The last item in the nav, below a rule. An ordinary white card whose rows carry the consequence in figures and a bordered red-text button; the typed confirmation lives in alert-dialog, not here.

behaviour: Clicking a section navigates. The pane swaps, focus moves into the new section's heading, the nav marks it with aria-current="page", and the scroll position of the pane resets while the nav does not move.
Each section commits on its own. Save writes that section and nothing else, the footer status line says so in words, and the last-changed line and its timestamp are rewritten from the response.

The dirty flag is set by input and change bubbling out of the section's own controls. While it is set, a click on any other section link is intercepted and the guard dialog opens with three answers — keep editing, discard and switch, save and switch — and beforeunload covers the tab closing.

A switch writes on change and answers into the status line under its block; it is never wired to the section's Save. A failed write reverts the switch to the value the server still holds and says which setting did not stick, naming it.

The numbering preview recomputes on every keystroke in the prefix, the separator and the width, and shows the next document number that would actually be issued. Changing the running number arms an acknowledgement that prints that number; Save stays refused until it is ticked.
The nav filter hides rows and updates a count. It never filters the pane, never changes which section is open, and clearing it restores the list with the open section still marked.
A permission matrix is a Save section, not a live one. Twenty-four boxes that each post on change is twenty-four requests nobody can reconcile, and no way to say what the state was before.

Below lg the nav stacks above the pane. At 390px the index and the section are two screens: choosing a section replaces the index, Back replaces the section, and focus is placed deliberately on both moves.
A section the signed-in user may not open is not in the nav and not in the pane. Nothing on the screen says it was removed, because a gap that announces itself is an invitation.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 is Settings. The open section's name is the h2 inside the pane and the blocks inside that section are h3 — the heading outline is how anybody skims a screen whose content changed without the page title changing.
Two navigation landmarks on one screen both need names, or the landmark list reads "navigation, navigation" and neither can be chosen. The shell's is Main and this one is Settings sections.

The section nav is links with aria-current="page", never role="tab" with aria-selected. They are two different promises: aria-current marks where you are among destinations, aria-selected marks which panel is showing, and a link wearing role="tab" tells a screen reader that arrows will switch panels and that Tab will jump into one, after which neither happens.

The pane is a <section> with aria-labelledby pointing at its own h2 and tabindex="-1", and it takes focus after a section change. Without it a nav click leaves the keyboard in the list and the next Tab walks the remaining thirty-nine sections instead of entering the one that was opened.

The save answers into a role="status" line inside the section footer. A save that changes nothing visible — a limit that was already 5,00,000, a tick that was already on — is announced by nothing at all otherwise, and the user presses Save again.

A toggle that writes on change carries its own role="status" line naming the setting, because reverting a switch after a failed write is script setting checked, and a programmatic change to checked is announced by nothing.

Every checkbox in a permission matrix carries an aria-label naming both axes — "Approve over ₹5,00,000 — Approver". Row and column headers are announced when a screen reader walks a table and not when somebody tabs through the controls inside one, which is how this screen is used.

The guard dialog is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, is trapped, and puts focus on Keep editing. Discard is never the focused answer: the dialog exists because something is about to be lost, and the safe answer is the one under the fingers.

The numbering preview is an <output> with aria-live="off". It recomputes on every keystroke and an <output> is a live region by default, so left on it reads the whole document number back one character at a time while the user is still typing the prefix.

On a phone the index and the section are two screens, and both moves place focus: choosing a section focuses its heading, Back focuses the row that was opened. A screen swap with focus left behind is a page that did not move for the person using it.
